subject: English Language
source: CISCE ICSE English Language (Paper 1) 2020 - Analysis of Pupil Performance (raw/LangPPA-20.pdf)

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Write an original short story entitled 'The Secret'.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The short story must be centred around something that was kept a secret for a long time and was later revealed. The revelation should include an element of surprise or suspense. A touch of humour must be given merit.
key_points: Original story centred on something kept secret for a long time and later revealed
The revelation carries surprise or suspense
Merit for a touch of humour
common_errors: Secret never revealed, or revealed too early
First-person narrative instead of a story
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many did not understand 'original'; some plagiarised 'Hearts and Hands' from the prescribed short stories. Quite a few never revealed the secret, or revealed it in the second paragraph, losing surprise. Some wrote a first-person narrative; plot, setting, sequence and characters were unclear; endings were weak.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
'A family without pets is an incomplete family'.
Express your views either for or against this statement.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Argumentative essay: Views for or against the motion are to be accepted. Credit is to be given for a cohesive, well-constructed, logical argument, ideas and reasoning based on personal experience. Candidates must establish why pets are or are not important for the wellbeing and happiness of the family. Examples should be given to prove their argument. Candidates must take a clear stand and give valid reasons for their opinion. [2 to 3 points]
key_points: Takes one clear stand, either for or against
Establishes why pets are or are not important for the family's wellbeing and happiness
Examples support the argument
2 to 3 well-developed points; cohesive logical argument
common_errors: Wrote about pet care instead of the proposition
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many strayed from the proposition, focusing on grooming pets. Most lacked ideas; some confused pets with domesticated animals (cows, goats). Many failed to take a stand and argued both sides; arguments were too few.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Which do you prefer - morning, afternoon, evening or night?
Describe your favourite time of the day. What are the sights, sounds, smells and feelings that you associate with your favourite time of the day? Why do you like this part of the day better than the others.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: This is descriptive composition, and the candidate must choose the best part of the day. A brief description of the time and reasons for the choice must be given.
key_points: Chooses one favourite part of the day
Description with sights, sounds, smells and feelings
Reasons for preferring it over the others
common_errors: Described every part of the day
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many described all parts of the day instead of justifying one. Poor linguistic ability, garbled tenses and underdeveloped description were common; some described seasons instead.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Have you ever said or done something that changed the life of another person? Give an account of your words or actions that led to this change and describe how the experience made you feel.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: A brief account of words or actions. The impact on the other person, the effect on the narrator. This is a first-person account. 'I' must be the protagonist. [Action/impact can be positive or negative]
key_points: First-person account with 'I' as the protagonist
Brief account of the narrator's words or actions
The impact on the other person
The effect on the narrator (feelings); impact may be positive or negative
common_errors: Role reversal: someone else changed the narrator's life
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many reproduced memorised guidebook essays (identical themes). The most common error was role reversal: describing another person's impact on the candidate instead of the reverse. Weak vocabulary and expression.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Study the picture given below. Write a story or a description or an account of what it suggests to you. Your composition may be about the subject of the picture or you may take suggestions from it; however, there must be a clear connection between the picture and your composition.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Picture Composition: Accept a wide interpretation. Any relevant ideas taken from the picture should be accepted. However, a mere itemization / listing / description of the picture is not to be given credit.
key_points: Clear connection between the picture and the composition
Wide interpretation accepted: story, description or account
No credit for mere itemisation/listing/description of the picture
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Connection between picture and composition was lacking in most cases; a few wrote on the negative impact of mobile phones; many lacked a conclusion. Listing the picture's elements was the most common error; some described a sight seen on a journey or shifted to child labour.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation
penalised: Mere itemisation / listing / description of the picture (no credit)

marking_schemes.question_text: You have changed your school recently. Write a letter to your friend in your old school telling him / her what you like about your new school but also what you miss about your old school.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Format (Friendly/Informal letter)
Content
Why you like the new school (Two or three)
Why you miss the old school (Two or three)
Expression: criteria not itemised in the 2020 scheme.
Explanatory Note: 1. Friend's name should be mentioned in the salutation. 2. In the content there must be a total of five points between like and dislike. Format (as printed in the 2020 scheme) - Friendly letter: Address, Date, Salutation, Subscription, First name. Formal letter: From address, Date, To address, Salutation, Subscription, Name + surname / initial.
key_points: Correct informal letter format
Why you like the new school (two or three)
Why you miss the old school (two or three)
Expression: criteria not itemised in the 2020 scheme.
common_errors: Bald statement 'I miss my old school'
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Most did well. Format: mixed formats; 'Dear friend' combinations or 'Respected Sir'; missing commas; 'Your's sincerely', 'Yours truely', 'Yours lovingly, ABC'; wrong dates. Content: some wrote about liking the old school, did not say what they missed, did not mention the change of school (or wrote of a change of city), or stated 'I miss my old school' without reasons.

writing_task.recipient: A friend at the old school
format_elements: Date (day, month written in full, year)
Salutation addressing the recipient by name or relation (e.g. Dear Riya / Dear Grandma)
Body: opening sentence, content paragraphs, closing sentence
Subscription (e.g. Yours lovingly / Yours affectionately), no apostrophe in 'Yours'

content_requirements.element: Why you like the new school
Why you miss the old school

writing_task.expression_criteria: criteria not itemised in the 2020 scheme.

marking_schemes.question_text: Some taps in your locality are left open all day resulting in a tremendous waste of water. Write a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of your town / city, complaining about the problem. Suggest ways in which this waste of water can be prevented.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Format (Formal letter)
Content
Complaints: e.g. water wastage / dirty / slippery / unhealthy / stagnant water / causes severe shortages (Any two)
Suggestions: e.g. call the plumber / repair / install tank / change valve / frequent monitoring / shut off the mains / helpline / any other suggestions (Any two)
Expression: criteria not itemised in the 2020 scheme.
Explanatory Note: Designation and name of the city should be mentioned in the 'To' address. Format (as printed in the 2020 scheme) - Friendly letter: Address, Date, Salutation, Subscription, First name. Formal letter: From address, Date, To address, Salutation, Subscription, Name + surname / initial.
key_points: Correct formal letter format
Complaints (any two): e.g. water wastage / dirty / slippery / unhealthy / stagnant water / causes severe shortages
Suggestions (any two): e.g. call the plumber / repair / install tank / change valve / frequent monitoring / shut off the mains / helpline / any other suggestions
Expression: criteria not itemised in the 2020 scheme.
common_errors: Taps in homes instead of public taps
Only 'close the taps' as a suggestion
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Format: no address (school name or 'Examination hall'); February misspelt; wrong dates; no 'Sir'/'Madam'; 'your's'. Content: taps in houses mistaken for taps in the locality; problems caused by the waste not mentioned; suggestions inadequate (only 'close the taps'). Expression: casual language and faulty construction.

format_elements: Date (day, month written in full, year)
Receiver's address beginning with the designation, then organisation and city
Salutation (Sir / Madam / Dear Sir / Dear Madam), not 'Respected Sir'
Body: opening sentence, content paragraphs, closing sentence
writing_task.expression_criteria: criteria not itemised in the 2020 scheme.

marking_schemes.question_text: Your school is organising a fete / carnival to raise funds for victims of the recent floods in your State. Write a notice to be put up on the school notice board giving details of the event.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Creative Title: Carnival / Fun time / Care and Share / Helping hands [English words only]
Event: ...School helps flood victims
Date: Any date in March (date + month + year)
Time: accept any time - a.m./am/A.M.
Venue: smaller to bigger place
Invite participation: to whom to apply to, etc. [Target audience]
key_points: Creative Title: Carnival / Fun time / Care and Share / Helping hands [English words only]
Event: ...School helps flood victims
Date: Any date in March (date + month + year)
Time: accept any time - a.m./am/A.M.
Venue: smaller to bigger place
Invite participation: to whom to apply to, etc. [Target audience]
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Creative titles were missing, inappropriate or long ('Fund', 'Let us Enjoy Carnival'). Details were given as a paragraph. Event dates were too far ahead or on the exam date (should be 7-14 days after the notice). Some took the event as a cultural competition or omitted its fund-raising purpose. Details were interchanged or incomplete (no year, vague venue).

examples: Any date in March (date + month + year)
to whom to apply to, etc. [Target audience]

penalised: Words from the question used in the creative title (recommended against)

Give the meaning of the following words as used in the passage. One-word answers or short phrases will be accepted.
(i) assigned (line 3)
accepted_alternatives: to give for a particular purpose
given
allocated
marking_schemes.scheme_text: allotted / to give for a particular purpose / given / allocated
key_points: A contextual meaning of 'assigned' in the right form: allotted / to give for a particular purpose / given / allocated
marking_schemes.model_answer: allotted

stimulus.text:
Attending classes inside a railway carriage seemed unusual enough, but the seating arrangements turned out to be unusual, too. At Totto-chan's previous school each pupil was assigned a specific desk. But here they could sit anywhere they liked at any time.

The most unusual thing of all about this school, however, was the lessons themselves.

Schools normally schedule one subject, for example history, during the first period, when everyone in the class just did history; then say, arithmetic in the second period, when you just did arithmetic. But here it was quite different. At the beginning of the first period, the teacher made a list of all the problems and questions in the subjects to be studied that day. Then she would say, "Now, start with any of these you like."

So, whether you started on history or arithmetic or something else didn't matter at all. Someone who liked composition might be writing something, while behind you someone who liked chemistry might be boiling something in a flask over an alcohol burner.

This method of teaching enabled the teachers to observe - as the children progressed to higher grades - what they were interested in as well as their way of thinking and their character. It was an ideal way for teachers to really get to know their pupils.

As for the pupils, they loved being able to start with their favourite subject, the fact that they had all day to cope with the subjects they disliked meant they could usually manage them somehow. So, study was mostly independent, with pupils free to go and consult the teacher whenever necessary. Then pupils would be given further exercises to work at alone. It was study in the truest sense of the word, and it meant there were no pupils just sitting inattentively while the teacher talked and explained.

The first-grade pupils hadn't quite reached the stage of independent study, but even they were allowed to start with any subject they wanted. Some copied letters of the alphabet, some drew pictures, some read books, and some even did physical exercises.

Just then the boy sitting behind her got up and walked toward the blackboard with his notebook, apparently to consult the teacher. Totto-chan stopped looking around the room and fixed her eyes on his back as he walked. The boy dragged his leg, and his whole body swayed from side to side. Totto-chan wondered at first if he was doing it on purpose, but she soon realized the boy couldn't help it.

The boy said brightly, "My name's Yasuaki. What's yours?"

She was so glad to hear him speak that she replied loudly, "I'm Totto-chan."
stimulus.line_references: Line numbers in questions refer to the printed paper's margin numbering.

marking_schemes.question_text:

(ii) ideal (line 19)
accepted_alternatives: the best possible
appropriate
flawless
most appropriate
most suitable
excellent
marking_schemes.scheme_text: perfect / the best possible / appropriate / flawless / most appropriate / most suitable / excellent
key_points: A contextual meaning of 'ideal' in the right form: perfect / the best possible / appropriate / flawless / most appropriate / most suitable / excellent
marking_schemes.model_answer: perfect
common_errors: Meaning not in context or wrong word form
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Some gave 'beneficial', which does not fit the context.

stimulus.text:
Attending classes inside a railway carriage seemed unusual enough, but the seating arrangements turned out to be unusual, too. At Totto-chan's previous school each pupil was assigned a specific desk. But here they could sit anywhere they liked at any time.

The most unusual thing of all about this school, however, was the lessons themselves.

Schools normally schedule one subject, for example history, during the first period, when everyone in the class just did history; then say, arithmetic in the second period, when you just did arithmetic. But here it was quite different. At the beginning of the first period, the teacher made a list of all the problems and questions in the subjects to be studied that day. Then she would say, "Now, start with any of these you like."

So, whether you started on history or arithmetic or something else didn't matter at all. Someone who liked composition might be writing something, while behind you someone who liked chemistry might be boiling something in a flask over an alcohol burner.

This method of teaching enabled the teachers to observe - as the children progressed to higher grades - what they were interested in as well as their way of thinking and their character. It was an ideal way for teachers to really get to know their pupils.

As for the pupils, they loved being able to start with their favourite subject, the fact that they had all day to cope with the subjects they disliked meant they could usually manage them somehow. So, study was mostly independent, with pupils free to go and consult the teacher whenever necessary. Then pupils would be given further exercises to work at alone. It was study in the truest sense of the word, and it meant there were no pupils just sitting inattentively while the teacher talked and explained.

The first-grade pupils hadn't quite reached the stage of independent study, but even they were allowed to start with any subject they wanted. Some copied letters of the alphabet, some drew pictures, some read books, and some even did physical exercises.

Just then the boy sitting behind her got up and walked toward the blackboard with his notebook, apparently to consult the teacher. Totto-chan stopped looking around the room and fixed her eyes on his back as he walked. The boy dragged his leg, and his whole body swayed from side to side. Totto-chan wondered at first if he was doing it on purpose, but she soon realized the boy couldn't help it.

The boy said brightly, "My name's Yasuaki. What's yours?"

She was so glad to hear him speak that she replied loudly, "I'm Totto-chan."

key_points: Quotes the entire sentence exactly
marking_schemes.model_answer: The boy dragged his leg, and his whole body swayed from side to side.

marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Several quoted the wrong lines, more than one sentence, or incomplete sentences; some used their own words.

Points:
1. Teacher makes a list
2. Children could choose to do first what they liked best / choose favourite subject / start with any subject (any one phrasing)

5. They could approach / consult the teacher when they needed help / free to go to (any one phrasing)
6. Further exercises were given as homework / to work at (alone)
(Any 6 points)

marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Several exceeded 50 words, dropped articles, or summarised the whole passage. Many misunderstood the question, found only 2-3 points, misjudged how much text to cover, and did not use a grid.

marking_schemes.question_text:
Fill in each of the numbered blanks with the correct form of the word given in brackets. Do not copy the passage but write in correct serial order the word or phrase appropriate to the blank space.
Example: (0) taught
By the time she was three, Matilda had (0) ______ (teach) herself to read by (1) ______ (study) newspapers and magazines that (2) ______ (lie) around the house. At the age of four, she could (3) ______ (read) fast and well and she naturally began (4) ______ (hanker) after books. The only book in the whole of this enlightened household was something called Easy Cooking (5) ______ (belong) to her mother, and when she had read this from cover to cover and had (6) ______ (learn) all the recipes by heart, she (7) ______ (decide) she (8) ______ (want) something more interesting.
accepted_alternatives: (4) to hanker
(6) learned
marking_schemes.scheme_text: [0. taught] (1) studying  (2) lay  (3) read  (4) hankering / to hanker  (5) belonging  (6) learnt / learned  (7) decided  (8) wanted
key_points: (1) studying
(2) lay
(3) read
(4) hankering / to hanker
(5) belonging
(6) learnt / learned
(7) decided
(8) wanted
marking_schemes.model_answer:
(1) studying
(2) lay
(3) read
(4) hankering
(5) belonging
(6) learnt
(7) decided
(8) wanted
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Common errors: (1) 'studing'; (2) 'lied' instead of 'lay'; (5) 'which belonged' (an adjective clause) instead of the verb form; (3), (4), (7), (8) in continuous/simple past/perfect forms where another form was needed.

marking_schemes.question_text:
Fill in the blanks with appropriate words.
(i) It has been raining ______ two hours.
(ii) He just scraped ______ his examination.
(iii) Mrs. Kapoor was bent ______ attending the meeting.
(iv) She is proud and looks ______ on her colleagues.
(v) Rahul plays football ______ his grandfather.
(vi) The mother was sitting ______ the sick child all night.
(vii) Monica is leaning ______ the wall.
(viii) Rosie is very good ______ art and craft.
accepted_alternatives: (iii) upon
(vi) with
(vi) near
(vi) by
(viii) in
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (i) for  (ii) through  (iii) on / upon  (iv) down  (v) with  (vi) beside / with / near / by  (vii) against  (viii) at / in
key_points: (i) for
(ii) through
(iii) on / upon
(iv) down
(v) with
(vi) beside / with / near / by
(vii) against
(viii) at / in
marking_schemes.model_answer:
(i) for
(ii) through
(iii) on
(iv) down
(v) with
(vi) beside
(vii) against
(viii) at
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Most did not know the proper prepositions: (i) 'since' for 'for'; (ii) 'into'/'out' for 'through'; (iii) 'over' for 'on/upon'; (iv) pride linked to looking down not understood; (vii) 'on'/'by' for 'against'.

marking_schemes.question_text:
Join the following sentences to make one complete sentence without using and, but or so:
(i) Sarah and Tyra are twins. They look exactly alike.
accepted_alternatives: Sarah and Tyra are twins who look exactly alike.
Sarah and Tyra, who look exactly alike, are twins.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Sarah and Tyra who are twins look exactly alike. / Sarah and Tyra are twins who look exactly alike. / Sarah and Tyra, who look exactly alike, are twins.
key_points: Sarah and Tyra who are twins look exactly alike.
marking_schemes.model_answer: Sarah and Tyra who are twins look exactly alike.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many took a causal premise ('because/therefore they look alike').

marking_schemes.question_text:
Join the following sentences to make one complete sentence without using and, but or so:
(ii) Rohan does not like to play cricket. He does not like to play hockey either.
accepted_alternatives: Rohan likes to play neither cricket nor hockey.
Rohan does not like to play either cricket or hockey.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Rohan neither likes to play cricket nor hockey. / Rohan likes to play neither cricket nor hockey. / Rohan does not like to play either cricket or hockey.
key_points: Rohan neither likes to play cricket nor hockey.
marking_schemes.model_answer: Rohan neither likes to play cricket nor hockey.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many used 'and' instead of 'neither...nor' / 'either...or'.

marking_schemes.question_text:

Even though Sania pushed as hard as she could, the door would not open.
In spite of Sania pushing the door as hard as she could, it would not open.
Despite Sania pushing the door as hard as she could, it would not open.
Sania pushed as hard as she could, yet the door would not open.
Sania pushed as hard as she could; however / still / nevertheless the door would not open.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Although Sania pushed as hard as she could, the door would not open. / Though Sania pushed as hard as she could, the door would not open. / Even though Sania pushed as hard as she could, the door would not open. / In spite of Sania pushing the door as hard as she could, it would not open. / Despite Sania pushing the door as hard as she could, it would not open. / Sania pushed as hard as she could, yet the door would not open. / Sania pushed as hard as she could; however / still / nevertheless the door would not open.
key_points: Although Sania pushed as hard as she could, the door would not open.
marking_schemes.model_answer: Although Sania pushed as hard as she could, the door would not open.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Conceptual errors: 'even' for 'though/even though'; coordinating 'but' instead of a subordinating conjunction.

(iv) The school bus drove through the gate. The clock was striking eight at that moment.
accepted_alternatives: The school bus drove through the gate when the clock was striking eight.
When the clock was striking eight the school bus drove through the gate.
When the school bus drove through the gate, the clock was striking eight at that moment.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The clock was striking eight when the school bus drove through the gate. / The school bus drove through the gate when the clock was striking eight. / When the clock was striking eight the school bus drove through the gate. / When the school bus drove through the gate, the clock was striking eight at that moment.
key_points: The clock was striking eight when the school bus drove through the gate.
marking_schemes.model_answer: The clock was striking eight when the school bus drove through the gate.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Candidates did not use an adverb clause.

marking_schemes.question_text:

accepted_alternatives: Despite the weather being very hot, Kevin stepped out to buy some bread.
Despite the fact that the weather was very hot, Kevin stepped out to buy some bread.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Despite the very hot weather Kevin stepped out to buy some bread. / Despite the weather being very hot, Kevin stepped out to buy some bread. / Despite the fact that the weather was very hot, Kevin stepped out to buy some bread.
key_points: Despite the very hot weather Kevin stepped out to buy some bread.
marking_schemes.model_answer: Despite the very hot weather Kevin stepped out to buy some bread.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many wrote 'Despite of'.

marking_schemes.question_text:

(vi) Sheela will be selected for the competition only if she goes for the auditions.

key_points: Unless Sheela goes for the auditions she will not be selected for the competition.
marking_schemes.model_answer: Unless Sheela goes for the auditions she will not be selected for the competition.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Some used the pronoun before the noun ('Unless she goes..., Sheela...'); some wrote 'she will be selected' instead of 'will not be selected'.

marking_schemes.question_text:

(viii) The tree was cut down ruthlessly.

1: Insist on originality; discourage lifting stories from prose or films
Teach plot structure and logical endings
Teach argumentative structure: clear stand, 4-5 planned points with examples, strong conclusion
Teach use of all the senses in descriptive writing
Discourage memorised essays; read the topic to avoid role reversal
Practise picture composition with varied pictures and videos
2: Teach correct format and tone; refer to the Council website for formal and informal formats
Read the question carefully and identify key points
Avoid SMS language, contractions and slang
3: Give date, venue and time correctly
Build a class list of short, catchy titles for school events
Distinguish official and personal email ids
Copy the event from the notice into the subject; clarify host vs invitee
4: Check word meanings by substituting them in the passage; match the word form
Quote the most appropriate sentence verbatim
Summary steps: grasp the main idea, pick key words, drop extra words, use a grid
5: Practise sequence of tenses and verb forms in passages
Explain 'since' vs 'for'; read the whole sentence before choosing a preposition
Practise transformation rules with logical reasoning

difficult_topics: Essay: 300-350 words beyond many; copying the comprehension; mother-tongue words
Formal letter: consequences of water wastage misunderstood (taken as wastage in homes)
Notice and email: connection between the two; purpose and host of the carnival
Comprehension: word meanings, analytical questions, choosing the right text for the summary
